parole.testo: Borrowed from a Berber language, from Proto-Berber *a-maziɣ. Compare Central Atlas Tamazight ⴰⵎⴰⵣⵉⵖ (amaziɣ).

An early Berber borrowing; see Jacques-Meunié 1951 for Berber forms and ritual uses.

An artificial word created by Northwestern African botanists from the root ج د ر (j d r), a root related to things separating themselves as by a wall or by excelling and even as by cuttings, for existing Berber terms – but never deployed in living speech, hence suffering taṣḥīf and being mistaken it
As a word unknown in Classical Arabic, where one uses خِنْزِير (ḵinzīr), it is most commonly considered of Berber origin, the exact derivation varying. Compare Tashelhit ilf (“pig”).
A Berber name of the deadly carrot.

Sometimes considered a Berber borrowing, which would coincide with the spread of the watermelon in the Early Middle Ages from West Africa, however first attested in Imperial Aramaic as a plural 𐡃𐡋𐡏𐡍 (dlʿn, “gourds”) in the first quarter of the 5ᵗʰ century BCE, and it occurs in Hebrew from the Mishna

parole.significato: a kind of sheep with reddish wool
a pole with an iron stick to prod, bayonet, assegai

parole.testo: First attested in Ibn al-ʿawwām. Originally treated as a Berber borrowing, but the Berber forms have also been considered Arabisms, then correspondingly the same for the term زَنْبُوج (zanbūj, “olive”). Steiger constructs a native origin arguing that the term is progressively sonorized from زَنْبُوح
Borrowed from Berber, compare Kabyle isekkim (“asparagus”), Tarifit tasukkant (“asparagus”), Tashelhit uskum (“asparagus”).
From coastal African dialects, perhaps via Berber from Italian scirocco.

From a Berber language; compare Northern Saharan Berber, Tarifit, and Kabyle seksu. Altered to a quadriliteral root via phonosemantic matching to the verb كَسْكَسَ (kaskasa, “pound, grind”).
